In the winter of nineteen fifty nine, nine young hikers set up their tent on a snowy mountain in Russia.
That night, something made all nine of them cut their way out of the tent, from the inside.
They ran out into the dark, into minus thirty degrees, some of them without shoes.
None of them came back.
When searchers found them weeks later, the story only got stranger.
Some had serious injuries, but no signs of a fight.
Their clothes had traces of radiation.
And the official report said they were killed by a compelling natural force.
For sixty years, nobody could explain what happened.
Today, we'll go through everything that was found, every big theory, and the answer that scientists finally gave.
And why some people still don't believe it.
This is the mystery of the Dyatlov Pass.
Part one. The hikers.
It's January nineteen fifty nine, in the Soviet Union.
A group of students and graduates from a university in the city of Sverdlovsk are planning a winter trip.
Their leader is Igor Dyatlov, a twenty three year old engineering student.
He's smart, careful, and already an experienced hiker.
The plan is to ski across the northern Ural Mountains to a peak called Otorten.
It's a hard route, given the highest difficulty rating at the time.
About sixteen days of skiing, through deep snow, in brutal cold.
But this group knew what they were doing.
Most of them were in their early twenties. Seven men, and two women.
Igor Dyatlov. Zinaida Kolmogorova. Lyudmila Dubinina.
Alexander Kolevatov. Rustem Slobodin. Yuri Krivonischenko.
Yuri Doroshenko. And Nikolai Thibeaux-Brignolle.
Friends, classmates, and experienced skiers.
And there was one older member, a thirty seven year old named Semyon Zolotaryov, a war veteran and an experienced guide.
At first, there were ten of them.
But a few days into the trip, one of them, Yuri Yudin, got sick.
His back and legs were hurting, and he couldn't keep going.
So he said goodbye, and turned back.
He didn't know it then, but that goodbye saved his life.
He would be the only one of the group to grow old.
Part two. The last night.
The nine remaining hikers kept going.
We know a lot about those days, because they kept diaries, and took photographs.
The photos show a happy group. Laughing, joking, skiing through the forest.
They even wrote a funny handmade newspaper, about life on the trail.
They called it the Evening Otorten.
One of the jokes in it said that scientists had proven the snowman exists, and that it lives in the northern Urals, near Otorten.
A joke that sounds a lot less funny today.
On the first of February, they started climbing the slope of a mountain the local Mansi people called Kholat Syakhl.
The name is often translated as Dead Mountain.
The weather was getting worse. Strong winds. Snow blowing everywhere.
So in the late afternoon, they stopped on the open slope, and set up camp.
They dug into the snow, put up their big tent, and ate dinner.
One of the last photos from their cameras shows them digging the spot for the tent, in the blowing snow.
And then, sometime that night, something went terribly wrong.
Part three. The tent.
The group was supposed to send a telegram when they finished the trip, around the twelfth of February.
That day came and went. No message.
At first, nobody worried. Trips like this were often late.
But by the twentieth, their families were scared, and a search began.
Students, soldiers, police, and planes all joined in.
On the twenty sixth of February, searchers found the tent.
It was half buried in snow.
And it had been cut open.
Not from the outside. From the inside.
Somebody had slashed through the fabric with a knife, to get out fast.
Why not just use the entrance?
Maybe it was blocked. Maybe it was too slow, with nine people crawling out one by one.
Whatever was happening, they felt they had seconds to leave.
Inside the tent, almost everything was still there.
Their boots. Their warm coats. Their food. Their gear.
Outside, the searchers found footprints in the snow.
Eight or nine people, walking down the slope, away from the tent.
Some prints were from socks. Some from a single boot. Some from bare feet.
In minus thirty degrees.
And the prints didn't look like people running in panic. They looked like people walking in a line.
The footprints went down the mountain, toward the forest, about a mile away.
Then they disappeared.
Part four. The cedar tree.
At the edge of the forest, the searchers found a tall cedar tree.
Under it were the remains of a small fire.
And next to the fire, they found the first two hikers.
They were wearing only their underwear.
Branches of the tree were broken off, up to about five meters high.
As if someone had climbed it, maybe to look back toward the tent.
Then, between the cedar tree and the tent, they found three more.
Including Igor Dyatlov himself.
They were lying in the snow, spaced out, facing back up the slope.
As if they had been trying to get back to the tent, and the cold stopped them.
The doctors said these five died from the cold.
Hypothermia.
And here's something that sounds strange, but is real.
When people get extremely cold, their body can trick them.
In the last stages of hypothermia, a freezing person can suddenly feel like they're burning hot.
Some people even start taking off their clothes.
Doctors call it paradoxical undressing.
It may help explain why some of the hikers were found wearing so little.
Sad. But at least it made some kind of sense.
The other four were still missing.
And they wouldn't be found until May.
Part five. The ravine.
When the snow started to melt, the searchers found the last four hikers.
They were in a ravine, a little deeper in the forest, under about four meters of snow, near a small stream.
And these four were different.
Some of them were wearing clothes cut from their friends who had died earlier.
As if they had tried to keep each other warm.
And three of them had serious injuries.
Broken ribs. A badly fractured skull.
Injuries so strong, one doctor compared them to being hit by a car.
But there were no wounds on the skin. No signs of a fight.
Some of the injuries looked very strange at first.
But later, experts said that weeks in the cold water of the stream explained a lot of that.
And then, one more thing.
When some of the clothes were tested, they showed traces of radiation.
Not a deadly amount. But enough to make people ask questions.
Part six. A compelling natural force.
In May nineteen fifty nine, the investigation was closed.
The official cause of death was something very vague.
The report said the hikers died because of a compelling natural force they couldn't overcome.
That was it.
No real explanation.
The area was closed to hikers for a few years.
And the files were kept secret for decades.
In the Soviet Union, secrecy was normal. But to the families, it felt like something was being hidden.
And when information finally came out in the nineteen nineties, the theories exploded.
Part seven. The theories.
Over the years, people have come up with dozens of explanations.
Let's look at the big ones.
Theory one. An attack.
Some people first thought the local Mansi hunters attacked the group, for entering their land.
But there were no other footprints. Nothing was stolen. And the Mansi were known as peaceful.
This theory was ruled out quickly.
Theory two. A secret military test.
This was the Cold War, and the area was not far from places where weapons were tested.
Other people in the region reported seeing strange orange lights in the sky that winter.
Could a test have gone wrong, and scared the hikers out of the tent?
That might explain the radiation, and the secrecy.
But no proof of a test on that night has ever been found.
And many of the lights seen that winter were later linked to rocket launches.
Theory three. A sound you can't hear.
Some scientists suggested that strong wind around the mountain could create infrasound.
A very low sound that humans can't hear, but that can cause panic, fear, and confusion.
It's a creative idea. But it's very hard to prove.
And then there are the wilder ones.
A yeti. Aliens. A spy mission gone wrong.
None of them have real evidence.
But they show how badly people wanted an answer.
And for sixty years, there wasn't one.
Part eight. The radiation.
Let's go back to the radiation, because it's the clue that makes this case feel so creepy.
It sounds like proof of something secret.
But there may be a simple answer.
One of the hikers, Yuri Krivonischenko, had worked at a nuclear plant.
Some of the clothes may have come from people who worked around radioactive materials.
And the traces were small.
Not enough to hurt anyone.
So the radiation might be a scary detail, with a boring explanation.
Part nine. The answer?
In twenty nineteen, Russian prosecutors reopened the case.
But they said they would only look at natural explanations.
An avalanche, a snow slab, or a hurricane.
Crimes, secret weapons, and aliens were ruled out from the start.
Some of the families were unhappy about that. They wanted every possibility checked.
And in twenty twenty, they announced their answer.
An avalanche.
But not the kind you're probably imagining.
Not a huge wall of snow crashing down the mountain.
Something smaller, and quieter.
A slab avalanche.
Here's how it works.
When the hikers set up camp, they dug a flat spot into the slope.
That cut weakened the snow above them.
During the night, strong winds kept piling more snow on top.
Until a block of hard snow, a slab, broke loose, and slid onto the tent.
Not enough to bury it. But enough to crush part of it, and to terrify them.
In the dark, the hikers would have thought a much bigger avalanche was coming.
So they cut their way out, and got away from the slope as fast as they could.
They planned to come back once it was safe.
But in the dark and the storm, they couldn't find the tent again.
In twenty twenty one, two Swiss scientists, Johan Gaume and Alexander Puzrin, tested this idea with computer models.
They even used snow simulation code from the animated movie Frozen.
Their results showed that a slab like this could happen on that slope.
And that a block of heavy, hard snow could cause the kinds of injuries the hikers had, if they were lying down in the tent.
Part ten. Why people still don't believe it.
So, is the mystery solved?
Many people say yes.
But many others still aren't convinced.
They point out that the searchers didn't report clear signs of an avalanche.
The tent was still standing in places, not flattened.
And the slope wasn't very steep.
Supporters of the avalanche theory say a slab can be small, and that the wind could have hidden the signs in the weeks before the searchers arrived.
And the injuries in the ravine?
Some experts think those four fell onto rocks in the ravine, while trying to dig a snow shelter in the dark.
Every theory explains some parts.
But for some people, none of them explain everything.
Part eleven. What really happened?
Here's what most experts think today.
Something frightened the hikers in the night. Most likely, snow sliding onto the tent.
They escaped fast, without time to dress.
They went down to the forest, to get out of the wind, and built a fire.
Some tried to get back to the tent, for their clothes and supplies, and froze on the way.
Others tried to build a shelter in the ravine, and were hurt when the snow or rocks gave way.
And the fire under the cedar tree shows they didn't give up.
They broke branches, gathered wood, and tried to survive the night together.
Some even gave their clothes to the others.
It's a story of nine people who made fast choices in terrible conditions.
And who, in the end, tried to take care of each other.
Not monsters. Not aliens. Just the mountain, the cold, and the dark.

Yuri Yudin, the hiker who turned back, lived until twenty thirteen.
He spent much of his life wondering what happened to his friends.
He once said that if he could ask God just one question, it would be what really happened that night.
Today, the place where they died is called the Dyatlov Pass, after their leader.
